<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\ \ \label{th1} Suppose that $G$ is a group. Then every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of $G$ is a TI-subgroup if and only of
one of the following statements holds.

$(1)$ every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of $G$ is normal;

$(2)$ $G={Z_p}^m\rtimes(Q_8\rtimes H)$ is a Frobenius group with kernel ${Z_p}^m$ and complement $Q_8\rtimes H$, where $m>1$, $p$ is the largest prime divisor of $|G|$, $H$ is a cyclic group of odd order, $Q_8\rtimes H$ acts irreducibly on ${Z_p}^m$ and $[Q_8,H]\neq 1$,
every non-cyclic maximal subgroup of  $Q_8\rtimes H$ contains $Q_8$, every cyclic maximal subgroup of $Q_8\rtimes H$ is a conjugate of $Z(Q_8)\times H$ and ${Z_p}^m\rtimes(Z(Q_8)\times H)$ is supersolvable.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\ \ \label{c1} Suppose that $G$ is a non-solvable group. Then every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of $G$ is a TI-subgroup if and only if every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of $G$ is normal.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\ \ \label{r1} {\rm In Theorem~\ref{th1} ${Z_p}^m\rtimes(Z(Q_8)\times H)$ is supersolvable implies that $Z(Q_8)\times H\lesssim Z_{p-1}$.}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\ \ \label{r2} {\rm Let $G\cong(Z_7\times Z_7)\rtimes(Q_8\rtimes Z_3)\cong (Z_7\times Z_7)\rtimes\rm SL(2,3)$, where $Q_8\rtimes Z_3$ is a subgroup of ${\rm Aut}(Z_7\times Z_7)\cong\rm GL(2,7)$
and $Q_8\rtimes Z_3$ acts irreducibly on $Z_7\times Z_7$.
It is easy to see that every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of $G$ is either normal or a Frobenius complement of $G$ which is a conjugate of $Q_8\rtimes Z_3$.}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\ \ \label{r3} {\rm Note that a group in which every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup is normal might not be solvable. For example, let $G\cong{\rm Aut}(\rm SL(3,2))$. Then
${\rm Aut}(\rm SL(3,2))$ has a unique non-supersolvable maximal subgroup which is isomorphic to $\rm SL(3,2)$ and $\rm SL(3,2)$ is non-solvable.}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\ \ \label{r4} {\rm If every non-supersolvable maximal subgroup of a group $G$ is normal, we cannot get that $G$ is either $q$-nilpotent
or $q$-closed for each prime divisor $q$ of $|G|$. For example, let $G\cong S_4$, the symmetric group of degree 4. It is easy to see that $G$ is neither $q$-nilpotent nor $q$-closed whenever $q=2$ or 3.}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\ \ \label{r5} {\rm It is easy to show that a group in which every non-supersolvable subgroup is normal is solvable by analyzing the counterexample of the smallest order. Then
a group in which every non-supersolvable subgroup is a TI-subgroup is solvable combining Theorem~\ref{th1}.}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
